**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 79, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 3):**

Surah al-Nazi'at is Meccan by scholarly consensus (ijma'). It has forty-five or forty-six verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By those who drag out with violence, and those who draw out gently, and those who glide swiftly, and those who race ahead, and those who direct affairs. On the day when the quaking one quakes, followed by the following one. Hearts that day will be trembling, their eyes humbled.﴾

﴿They say: "Shall we indeed be returned to our former state? Even when we are decayed bones?" They say: "That would then be a losing return." But it will be only one shout, and at once they will be on the surface of the earth.﴾

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿By those who drag out with violence﴾. He swears by these things He mentioned that the Resurrection is true. "Those who drag out" (al-nazi'at) are the angels who pull out the souls of the disbelievers. This was said by ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him. Likewise Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Masruq and Mujahid said: they are the angels who pull out the souls of the children of Adam. Ibn Masʿud said: he means the souls of the disbelievers, which the Angel of Death pulls out of their bodies from beneath every hair and beneath the nails and the soles of the feet, pulling them out like a skewer pulled from wet wool. "Ighraq" means he drowns them, that is, he sends them back into their bodies, then pulls them out again; this is his work with the disbelievers. Ibn ʿAbbas said the same. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: their spirits are pulled out, then drowned, then burned, then cast into the Fire. It has also been said: the disbeliever sees his soul at the time of its extraction as if it were drowning. al-Suddi said: "those who drag out" are the souls as they sink into the chests. Mujahid said: it is death, which pulls out the souls. al-Hasan and Qatadah said: they are the stars, which are drawn from one horizon to another, meaning they move, from the expression "nazaʿa ilayhi" (he went toward it), or from the expression "nazaʿat al-khayl" (the horses ran). "Gharqan" means they sink, set, and rise from one horizon to another. This was said by Abu ʿUbayda, Ibn Kaysan and al-Akhfash. It has also been said: "those who drag out" are bows, which draw the arrows. This was said by ʿAta and ʿIkrima. "Gharqan" means "ighraqan" (drawing to the utmost). Drawing a bow to its utmost (ighraq) means pulling it until it reaches its full extent, until it reaches the arrowhead. It is said: "aghraqa fi al-qawsi," meaning he completed its draw, which happens when the string reaches the notch next to the arrowhead, around which it is wound. "Al-istighraq" means full comprehensiveness. The inner membrane of an eggshell is called "ghirqi'." It has also been said: they are the warriors who shoot arrows. I say: this and the previous interpretation amount to the same thing, because when He swears by the bows, what is meant is those who draw them, in honour of them. This is like His saying: ﴿By the charging steeds, panting﴾ [al-ʿAdiyat: 1]. And Allah knows best. By "ighraq" He intended exaggeration in drawing, and this applies to all the interpretations of it. It has also been said: they are wild animals that drag away from the pasture and flee. This was related by Yahya ibn Salam. The meaning of "gharqan" is then: going far away while drawing.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who draw out gently﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: this means the angels who ease the soul of the believer and take it, as a tether is loosed from the foot of a camel when it is untied. al-Farraʾ related this view and then said: what I have heard from the Arabs is that they say "unshitat" (it was loosed), and "ka-annama unshita min ʿiqal" (as if it were loosed from a tether). Its binding is its "nashṭ" (tying), and the one who ties is "nashit"; when you tie a rope to a camel's foot, you have "nashatah," so you are "nashit," and when you untie it, you have "anshatah," and you are "munshit." Also from Ibn ʿAbbas: they are the souls of believers at death, which become eager to leave, because no believer is facing death without Paradise being shown to him before he dies, so he sees what Allah has prepared for him of wives and family, the dark-eyed houris. They call him to it, so his soul is eager to leave and go to them. Also from him, he said: this means the souls of disbelievers and hypocrites, which are drawn out as the sinew is drawn out from which the arrow is strung. "Al-ʿaqab," with a vowel on the first letter, is the sinew from which bowstrings are made, singular "ʿaqabah." It is said of it: "ʿaqaba al-sahm wa al-qadah wa al-qaws ʿaqban," meaning he wound something of it around it. "Al-nashṭ" is pulling quickly. From it comes "al-unshuṭah," a knot that is easily loosened when pulled, like the knot of a belt. Abu Zayd said: "nashaṭtu al-habl, unshiṭuhu nashṭan" means I tied it with a slip-knot, and "anshaṭtu al-habl" means I loosened it, and "anshaṭtu al-habl" also means I stretched it until it came loose. al-Farraʾ said: "unshiṭa al-ʿiqal" means it was untied, and "nushiṭa" means the rope was tied on its two hands. al-Layth said: "anshaṭtuhu bi-unshuṭah wa unshuṭatayn" means I tightened it, and "anshaṭtu al-ʿiqal" means I stretched its knot until it came loose. He said: "nashiṭa" and "anshaṭa" are two dialects with the same meaning, and on this basis Ibn ʿAbbas's earlier statement is valid. Also from him: "al-nashiṭat" are the angels, because of their vigour; they go and come by Allah's command wherever they are. Also from him, and from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both: they are the angels who draw out the spirits of the disbelievers, from between the skin and the nails, until they bring them out of their bodies with force, through distress and grief, as wool is drawn out of an iron skewer. This comes from "nashṭ," meaning pulling. It is said: "nashaṭtu al-dalw, anshiṭuhā" (with a kasra) and "anshuṭuhā" (with a damma), meaning I drew out the bucket. al-Asmaʿi said: "bi'r anshāṭ" is a well whose bottom is near, from which the bucket is drawn with one pull. "Bi'r nashūṭ" is a well from which the bucket cannot be drawn until it has been pulled many times. Mujahid said: it is death, which draws out the soul of a person. al-Suddi said: they are the souls as they are drawn out from the feet. It has also been said: "al-nazi'at" are the hands of the warriors, or their souls, which draw the bows by drawing the arrows to their utmost, and "al-nashiṭat" are those who loosen the snares. "Awhaq" (plural of "wahq," a rope with a vowel on each letter, and it may be softened) is a rope with which camels and horses are tied so that they do not bolt; a slip-knot is put at its end. ʿIkrima and ʿAta said: "al-awhaq" are the ropes that loosen the arrows. From ʿAta, Qatadah, al-Hasan and al-Akhfash also: "al-nashiṭat" are the stars, which move from one horizon to another, that is, they go. This is also in al-Sihah. "Wa al-nashiṭati nashṭan" means the stars moving from one constellation to another, like a bull that is loosed from one land to another. Anxieties also move their owner about, as Himyan ibn Qahafa said:

*My worries have come to move me about the regions,*
*Sometimes to Syria with me, sometimes to Wasit.*

Abu ʿUbayda and ʿAta also said: "al-nashiṭat" are the wild beasts when they move from one land to another, just as worries move a person from one land to another. He recited Himyan's verse: "My worries..." to the end of the line. It has also been said: "wa al-nazi'at" refers to disbelievers, and "wa al-nashiṭat" refers to believers, since the angels draw out the spirit of the believer gently, and "nazʿ" is drawing with force, while "nashṭ" is drawing gently. It has also been said: both apply to disbelievers, and the two verses after them apply to believers at the moment of leaving this world.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who glide swiftly﴾. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they are the angels who carry the spirits of the believers, gliding. al-Kalbi said: they are the angels who take the spirits of the believers, like one who swims in water: at times he dips and at times he rises. They draw them out gently and easily, then leave them so that they may rest. Mujahid and Abu Salih said: they are the angels who descend from heaven swiftly by Allah's command, as a swift horse is called "sabih" when it speeds up in its running. Also from Mujahid: the angels swim in their descent and their ascent. Also from him: "al-sabihat" is death, which swims within the souls of the children of Adam. It has also been said: they are the warhorses, as ʿAntarah said:

*And the horses know, when they swim
Into the reservoirs of death, a swim.*

Imru al-Qays said:

*Swift-running, when the racing ones grow weary,
They raise dust with their hooves over the rough ground.*

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: they are the stars that swim in their orbits, and likewise the sun and the moon. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿each in an orbit they swim﴾. ʿAta said: they are the ships that sail upon the water. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "al-sabihat" are the spirits of believers that swim with longing for the meeting with Allah and His mercy when they leave the body.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who race ahead﴾. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they are the angels who outrun the devils with revelation to the Prophets, peace be upon them. This was also said by Masruq and Mujahid. Also from Mujahid and Abu Rawq: they are the angels who outrun the son of Adam with good and righteous deeds. It has also been said: they outrun the children of Adam to righteous deeds and record them. Also from Mujahid: death outruns the human being. Muqatil said: they are the angels who carry the spirits of believers swiftly to Paradise. Ibn Masʿud said: they are the souls of believers, which race to the angels who take them, having already seen the joy, out of longing for the meeting with Allah and His mercy. Similar to this is from al-Rabiʿ, who said: they are the souls which race to leave at death. Qatadah, al-Hasan and Maʿmar said: they are the stars, some of which outrun others in their course. ʿAta said: they are the horses that race to jihad. It has also been said: "al-sabiqat" may be the spirits that outrun the bodies to Paradise or to the Fire, as al-Mawardi said. Al-Jurjani said: Allah mentioned "fa-al-sabiqat" with "fa" because it is derived from what comes before it, meaning "and those who swim, and so outrun." You say: "qama fa-dhahaba" (he stood up and so went), which means that standing up was the cause of going; but if you say "qama wa-dhahaba" (he stood up and went), standing up is not the cause of going.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 79, verses 1–14 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Then by those who arrange affairs﴾. Al-Qushayri said: They agreed that what is meant is the angels. Al-Mawardi said: There are two opinions on this. The first is that they are the angels, which is the view of the majority (al-jumhur). The second opinion is that they are the seven planets. This was related by Khalid ibn Ma'dan from Mu'adh ibn Jabal. As for their arranging affairs, there are two views. The first is that they arrange their rising and their setting. The second is that they arrange what Allah Most High has decreed concerning them of the changes of conditions. Al-Qushayri also related this view in his tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), and said that Allah Most High linked much of the arrangement of the affairs of the world to the movements of the stars, so the arrangement was attributed to them, even though it is from Allah, just as a thing is named after what is adjacent to it. And on the view that what is meant by "those who arrange" is the angels, their arranging is their bringing down of the lawful and the unlawful and its details. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others. The arranging belongs to Allah, exalted be His praise, but when the angels brought it down, they were named after it, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 193], and as He Most High said: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, for he has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97]. That is, Gabriel brought it down upon the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ), while Allah, mighty and majestic, is the One who sent it down. Ata related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿those who arrange affairs﴾: they are the angels entrusted with arranging the conditions of the earth regarding the winds, the rains and other things. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabat said: The arrangement of the affairs of this world is entrusted to four: Gabriel, Michael, the Angel of Death, whose name is 'Izra'il, and Israfil. As for Gabriel, he is entrusted with the winds and the armies. As for Michael, he is entrusted with the rain and vegetation. As for the Angel of Death, he is entrusted with seizing souls on land and sea. As for Israfil, he descends with the command to them, and no angel is closer than Israfil to the Throne, and between him and the Throne is a distance of five hundred years. It was also said: that is, they were entrusted with matters which Allah made them aware of. From the beginning of the surah up to here is an oath which Allah swore by, and Allah may swear by whatever He wills of His creation, while we have no right to do so except by Him, mighty and majestic. The answer to the oath is implied, as if He said: "By those who pull out violently, and so-and-so, you will surely be resurrected and surely be called to account." It is left implied because the listeners know its meaning, as al-Farra' said. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿When we are bones, decayed, [will we be resurrected]?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 11], which serves as the answer to their saying: ﴿When we are bones, decayed, will we be resurrected?﴾, so He suffices with His saying: ﴿When we are bones, decayed?﴾. Some people said: The oath falls upon His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 26]. This is the choice of al-Tirmidhi Ibn 'Ali, meaning: in what I have recounted of the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the mention of Moses and Pharaoh, there is indeed a lesson for whoever fears. But the oath falls upon what is mentioned clearly and openly in the surah, which is more fitting and more worthy than bringing something that is not mentioned. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is ugly, because the speech has been long between them. It was also said: the answer to the oath is ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 15], because the meaning is: it has reached you. It was also said: the answer is ﴿On the day the quaking one quakes﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 6], on the assumption of "la-yawma tarjufu" (surely on the day it quakes), and the lam was omitted. It was also said: there is inversion in it, and its estimate is: "On the day the quaking one quakes, and the following one follows, and by those who pull out violently." Al-Sijistani said: It is possible that this is from inversion, as if he said: "So they will be in the wakeful ground, and by those who pull out violently." Ibn al-Anbari said: This is an error, because the fa' is not used to begin speech, and the first is the correct view. It was also said: the oath only falls upon the hearts of the people of the Fire becoming dry and their eyes being humbled, so the accusative of ﴿on the day the quaking one quakes﴾ is according to this meaning, but it did not fall upon it. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, hearts will be trembling on the day it quakes. It was also said: it is governed by an implied "remember". ﴿Tarjufu﴾ means it is agitated. ﴿Al-Rajifah﴾ means the agitated one. This is what 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: he said it is the earth, and ﴿al-Radifah﴾ is the Hour. Mujahid said: ﴿al-Rajifah﴾ is the earthquake, and ﴿the following one follows it﴾ is the Blast. He also said, and so did Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah: they are the two Blasts, that is, the two blowings of the Trumpet. The first causes everything to die by the permission of Allah Most High, and the second brings everything to life by the permission of Allah Most High. There came in a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Between them is forty years." Mujahid also said: ﴿al-Radifah﴾ is when the sky is split and the earth and mountains are carried and crushed into one crushing, and that is after the earthquake. It was also said: ﴿al-Rajifah﴾ is the shaking of the earth, and ﴿al-Radifah﴾ is another earthquake which destroys the earths. And Allah knows best. What has passed at the end of "al-Naml" [[See vol. 13, p. 239 onwards.]] contains sufficiency regarding the blowing into the Trumpet. The root of rajfah is movement. Allah Most High said: ﴿On the day the earth quakes﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 14]. The rajfah here is not from movement alone, but from their saying: "rajafa al-ra'du yarjufu rajfan wa rajifan," meaning the thunder made its sound and its movement, and from this comes "al-arajif" (rumours), because of the agitation of voices through them and the people spreading them. He said:
"O father of rumours, O son of baseness, you threaten me, / and in the rumours I thought baseness and weakness were." [[The poem is by Manazil ibn Rabi'ah al-Munqari, in satire of Ru'bah and al-'Ajjaj. The well-known version of the line, as in the grammar books such as Sharh al-Tasrih and others, is: "O father of the rajaz poems, O son of baseness, you threaten me, / and in the rajaz poems, I thought, is baseness and weakness." "Al-arajiz" is the plural of "urjuzah," meaning poems composed in the meter of rajaz. "Wa fi al-arajiz" is the predicate preceding the subject "al-lu'm," and the interposition of "khalt" between the subject and predicate cancels its governing, which is the point of evidence in the line for the grammarians. It was also said that the accusative is not impossible, on the basis that a subject is implied, meaning "as for".]]

And from Ubayy ibn Ka'b: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to stand up when a quarter of the night had passed, and then say: "O people, remember Allah. The Quaking one has come, the following one follows it. Death has come with what is in it." [[the hadith as quoted]]

﴿Hearts on that day will be trembling﴾, that is, fearful and anxious. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and the majority of the exegetes hold this view. Al-Suddi said: moving from their places. Its parallel is: ﴿when the hearts reach the throats﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. Al-Mu'arrikh said: anxious, hasty, agitated, not still. Al-Mubarrad said: agitated. The meanings are close, and what is meant is the hearts of the disbelievers. It is said: "wajafa al-qalb yajifu wajifan," when it pounds, just as it is said: "wajaba yajibu wajiban." From this comes "wajif" of the horse and the camel when running, and "al-iyjaf" means driving a mount to a swift journey. He said:
"They were replaced after a snorting of breath with a clatter, / and after long breath with galloping."

﴿Hearts﴾ is in the nominative as the subject, and ﴿trembling﴾ is its description. ﴿Their eyes are humbled﴾ is its predicate, like His saying: ﴿a believing slave is better than an idolater﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]. The meaning of ﴿humbled﴾ is broken and abased from the terror of what they see. Its parallel is: ﴿their eyes humbled, humiliation will cover them﴾ [al-Qalam: 43]. The meaning is "the eyes of their owners", so the genitive word was omitted.

﴿They say: "Shall we indeed be returned to the former state?"﴾, that is, these deniers who reject resurrection say, when it is said to them that you will be resurrected, saying with denial and wonder: "Shall we be returned after our death to the first state, so that we return living as we were before death?" This is like their saying: ﴿Shall we indeed be raised in a new creation?﴾. It is said: "raja'a fulan fi hafiratihi" and "'ala hafiratihi," meaning he returned from where he came. This was said by Qatadah. Ibn al-A'rabi recited:
"Ahafirah 'ala salaf wa shayb / ma'adha Allah min safah wa 'ar" [meaning: "Shall I return to baldness and grey hair? God forbid from foolishness and shame!"]
He says: "Shall I return to what I was in my youth of love-poetry and youthful folly, after I have grown grey and bald?" It is also said: "raja'a 'ala hafiratihi," that is, the path by which he came. Their proverb says: "al-naqd 'inda al-hafirah" (payment is at the first word). Ya'qub said: that is, at the first word. It is also said: "al-taqa al-qawm fa-qatalu 'inda al-hafirah," that is, at the moment they first met. It was also said: al-hafirah means the worldly life, meaning: shall we indeed be returned to this world so that we live as we were? The poet said:
"I swore I would never forget you, so know this, / until people are returned to the hafirah."

It was also said: al-hafirah is the earth in which their graves are dug, so it has the meaning of "the dug-up," like His saying: ﴿created from a gushing fluid﴾ [al-Tariq: 6] and ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21]. The meaning: shall we indeed be returned to our graves alive? This was said by Mujahid, al-Khalil and al-Farra'. It was also said: the earth is called al-hafirah because it is the place where hooves rest, just as the foot is called earth because it is on the earth. The meaning: shall we indeed return after death to the earth and walk on our feet? Ibn Zayd said: al-hafirah is the Fire, and he recited: ﴿That, then, would be a losing return﴾. Muqatil and Zayd ibn Aslam said: it is one of the names of the Fire. Ibn 'Abbas said: in the language of the Arabs, al-hafirah is the world. Abu Haywah recited: "al-hafirah" without alif, a shortened form of "al-hafir." It was also said: al-hafirah is the earth filled with the bodies of its dead, from their saying: "hafirat asnanuhu," when filth settles on its outside and inside. It is said: "fi asnanihi hafar," and "qad hafirat tahfir hafran," like "kasara yaksiru kasran," when its roots are spoiled. The Bani Asad say: "fi asnanihi hafar" with vowel movement, and "qad hafira" in the pattern of "ta'iba ta'aban." This is the worse of the two dialects, said in al-Sihah.

﴿When we are bones, decayed?﴾, that is, crumbling and disintegrating. It is said: "nakhara al-'azm" (with kasra), meaning it decayed and crumbled, and it is said: "'izam nakhirah." So the majority of the people of Madinah, Makkah, Syria and Basra recited it, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred it, because when we looked at the reports that mention bones, we found "nakhirah," not "nakhirah" with alif. Abu 'Amr and his son 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn al-Zubayr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr recited "nakhirah" with alif. Al-Farra', al-Tabari and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi preferred it, as it would match the ends of verses. In al-Sihah: "al-nakhir" among bones is that into which wind enters and then comes out of it, and it has a whistling sound. It is said: "ma biha nakhir," meaning there is no one in it. Ya'qub related this from al-Bahili. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "al-nakhirah" is that which has not yet been hollowed, meaning it has not yet decayed, and it must eventually become hollow. It was also said: "al-nakhir" is the hollowed one. It was also said: they are two dialects with one meaning, just as the Arabs say: "nakhira al-shay'" so it is "nakhir" and "nakhir," like their saying: "ta'ima fa-huwa tama' wa ta'im," "hadhira fa-huwa hadhir wa hadhar," "bakhila fa-huwa bakhil wa bakhil," "rafara wa fari." The poet said:
"The old man who was once fat stays on them, / he creeps on crooked legs with the nakhirat." [[ 'Uwaj: meaning legs.]]

In some tafsir: "nakhirah" with alif means decayed, and "nakhirah" means that wind passes through it, the reverse of the first. The poet said [[the poet is al-Hamadani on the day of al-Qadisiyyah]]:
"After I became bones, hollowed (nakhirah)."
Some said: al-nakhirah is that whose extremities have been eaten and whose middles remain, and al-nakhirah is that whose entirety has spoiled. Mujahid said: nakhirah means crumbled, just as He said: ﴿bones and dust﴾ [al-Isra': 49]. The "nukhrat al-rih," with a damma, is the intensity of its blowing. Al-nukhrah also and al-nukhrah, in the pattern of al-hamzah, is the front of the nose of a horse, a donkey or a pig. It is said: "hashsham nukhratahu," meaning he crushed its nose.

﴿They said: "Then that would be a losing return"﴾, that is, a futile return, false and vain, meaning it is not a return that succeeds. This was said by al-Hasan and others. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: ﴿losing﴾ for those who denied it. It was also said: meaning it is a return of loss, and the meaning is that its people are losers, just as it is said: "a profitable trade," meaning its owner profits. There is nothing more losing than a return that leads to the Fire. Qatadah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: meaning, if we return alive after death, we will surely be gathered to the Fire, and they only said this because they had been threatened with the Fire. Al-Karr means return. It is said: "karrahu" and "karra bi-nafsihi," transitive and intransitive. Al-karrah means one time, and its plural is al-karrat.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 79, verses 1–14 (part 3 of 3):

(فَإِنَّما هِيَ زَجْرَةٌ واحِدَةٌ) ﴿Then it will be but a single shout﴾. He, exalted is His praise, mentioned the ease of the resurrection for Him, saying: ﴿Then it will be but a single shout﴾. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A single blast." ﴿And behold, they will be awake upon the Sahirah﴾, that is, upon the surface of the earth, after they had been in its belly. Al-Farra' said: "It was named this because in it is the sleep and wakefulness of living beings." The Arabs call a desert and the surface of the earth "sahirah," meaning "possessing wakefulness," because one stays awake in it out of fear of it; so He described it by a quality of what is in it. Ibn 'Abbas and the exegetes cited the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

وَفِيهَا لَحْمُ سَاهِرَةٍ وَبَحْرٍ ... وَمَا فَاهُوا بِهِ لَهُمْ مُقِيمُ

And another said on the day of Dhi Qar, to his horse:

أَقْدَمُ مَحَاجَ إِنَّهَا الْأَسَاوِرَهْ ... وَلَا يَهُولَنَّكَ رِجْلٌ [[These verses belong to al-Hamdani on the day of al-Qadisiyya, and their mention has preceded. Muhajj: the name of the poet's horse. In al-Lisan, under the root (n-kh-r): "Aqdim akhā nahm." "Wa la yahawlannaka ru'us." In al-Samin: "badirah."]] نَادِرَهْ
فَإِنَّمَا قَصْرُكَ تُرْبُ السَّاهِرَهْ ... ثُمَّ تَعُودُ بَعْدَهَا فِي الْحَافِرَهْ
مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا صِرْتَ عِظَامًا نَاخِرَهْ

In al-Sihah: It is said: "al-Sahur" is the shadow of the Sahirah, which is the surface of the earth. From this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And behold, they will be upon the Sahirah﴾. Abu Kabir al-Hudhali said:

يَرْتَدْنَ سَاهِرَةً كَأَنَّ جَمِيمَهَا ... وَعَمِيمَهَا أَسْدَافُ لَيْلٍ مُظْلِمِ [[al-Jamim, with a jim: the plant that has sprouted and risen slightly but has not fully matured; al-'Amim: the complete, fully grown plant; al-Asdaf: plural of sadf, with a fathah, which is the darkness of the night.]]

It is also said: "al-Sahur" is like a sheath for the moon, into which it enters when it is eclipsed. They recited the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt [[The first half of the verse is: "la naqsa fihi ghayra anna khabay'ah"]]:

قَمَرٌ وَسَاهُورٌ يُسَلُّ وَيُغْمَدُ

And they recited, from another, describing a woman:

كَأَنَّهَا عِرْقُ سَامٍ عِنْدَ ضَارِبِهِ ... أَوْ شُقَّةٌ [[So it is in the copies of the original that are in our hands. What is in al-Lisan, under the root (s-h-r): "aw filqah."]] خَرَجَتْ مِنْ جَوْفٍ سَاهُورٍ

He means a split of the moon. [[This is what the Arabs claimed in the pre-Islamic period.]]

It was said: al-Sahirah is the white earth. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A land of silver, upon which Allah, exalted is His praise, was never disobeyed, which He created at that time." It was said: "A land which Allah renews on the Day of Resurrection." It was said: "al-Sahirah is the name of the seventh earth, which Allah, exalted is He, will bring forth, and upon which He will call the creatures to account, and that is when the earth will be replaced by another earth." Al-Thawri said: "al-Sahirah is the land of Sham." Wahb ibn Munabbih: "A mountain of Bayt al-Maqdis." 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'Atikah: "It is the name of a specific place on earth, in Sham, the region between the mountain of Ariha' and the mountain of Hassan [[Also mentioned by al-Tabari.]], which Allah extends however He wills." Qatadah: "It is Hell," that is, "then behold, these disbelievers are in Hell." It was only called sahirah because they will not sleep upon it at that time. It was also said: "al-Sahirah" means the desert at the edge of Hell, meaning they will be made to stand in the land of the Resurrection, and wakefulness will then persist. It is also said: "al-Sahirah is the white, level land, named so because the mirage flows over it," from the saying "'ayn sahirah," meaning a spring of flowing water; its opposite is "na'imah" (sleeping). Al-Ash'ath ibn Qays said:

وَسَاهِرَةٌ يُضْحِي السَّرَابُ مُجَلِّلًا ... لِأَقْطَارِهَا قَدْ جِئْتُهَا مُتَلَثِّمَا

Or because whoever travels through it does not sleep, out of fear of perishing.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 79, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 3):**

Surah al-Nazi'at is Meccan by scholarly consensus (ijma'). It has forty-five or forty-six verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By those who drag out with violence, and those who draw out gently, and those who glide swiftly, and those who race ahead, and those who direct affairs. On the day when the quaking one quakes, followed by the following one. Hearts that day will be trembling, their eyes humbled.﴾

﴿They say: "Shall we indeed be returned to our former state? Even when we are decayed bones?" They say: "That would then be a losing return." But it will be only one shout, and at once they will be on the surface of the earth.﴾

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿By those who drag out with violence﴾. He swears by these things He mentioned that the Resurrection is true. "Those who drag out" (al-nazi'at) are the angels who pull out the souls of the disbelievers. This was said by ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him. Likewise Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Masruq and Mujahid said: they are the angels who pull out the souls of the children of Adam. Ibn Masʿud said: he means the souls of the disbelievers, which the Angel of Death pulls out of their bodies from beneath every hair and beneath the nails and the soles of the feet, pulling them out like a skewer pulled from wet wool. "Ighraq" means he drowns them, that is, he sends them back into their bodies, then pulls them out again; this is his work with the disbelievers. Ibn ʿAbbas said the same. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: their spirits are pulled out, then drowned, then burned, then cast into the Fire. It has also been said: the disbeliever sees his soul at the time of its extraction as if it were drowning. al-Suddi said: "those who drag out" are the souls as they sink into the chests. Mujahid said: it is death, which pulls out the souls. al-Hasan and Qatadah said: they are the stars, which are drawn from one horizon to another, meaning they move, from the expression "nazaʿa ilayhi" (he went toward it), or from the expression "nazaʿat al-khayl" (the horses ran). "Gharqan" means they sink, set, and rise from one horizon to another. This was said by Abu ʿUbayda, Ibn Kaysan and al-Akhfash. It has also been said: "those who drag out" are bows, which draw the arrows. This was said by ʿAta and ʿIkrima. "Gharqan" means "ighraqan" (drawing to the utmost). Drawing a bow to its utmost (ighraq) means pulling it until it reaches its full extent, until it reaches the arrowhead. It is said: "aghraqa fi al-qawsi," meaning he completed its draw, which happens when the string reaches the notch next to the arrowhead, around which it is wound. "Al-istighraq" means full comprehensiveness. The inner membrane of an eggshell is called "ghirqi'." It has also been said: they are the warriors who shoot arrows. I say: this and the previous interpretation amount to the same thing, because when He swears by the bows, what is meant is those who draw them, in honour of them. This is like His saying: ﴿By the charging steeds, panting﴾ [al-ʿAdiyat: 1]. And Allah knows best. By "ighraq" He intended exaggeration in drawing, and this applies to all the interpretations of it. It has also been said: they are wild animals that drag away from the pasture and flee. This was related by Yahya ibn Salam. The meaning of "gharqan" is then: going far away while drawing.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who draw out gently﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: this means the angels who ease the soul of the believer and take it, as a tether is loosed from the foot of a camel when it is untied. al-Farraʾ related this view and then said: what I have heard from the Arabs is that they say "unshitat" (it was loosed), and "ka-annama unshita min ʿiqal" (as if it were loosed from a tether). Its binding is its "nashṭ" (tying), and the one who ties is "nashit"; when you tie a rope to a camel's foot, you have "nashatah," so you are "nashit," and when you untie it, you have "anshatah," and you are "munshit." Also from Ibn ʿAbbas: they are the souls of believers at death, which become eager to leave, because no believer is facing death without Paradise being shown to him before he dies, so he sees what Allah has prepared for him of wives and family, the dark-eyed houris. They call him to it, so his soul is eager to leave and go to them. Also from him, he said: this means the souls of disbelievers and hypocrites, which are drawn out as the sinew is drawn out from which the arrow is strung. "Al-ʿaqab," with a vowel on the first letter, is the sinew from which bowstrings are made, singular "ʿaqabah." It is said of it: "ʿaqaba al-sahm wa al-qadah wa al-qaws ʿaqban," meaning he wound something of it around it. "Al-nashṭ" is pulling quickly. From it comes "al-unshuṭah," a knot that is easily loosened when pulled, like the knot of a belt. Abu Zayd said: "nashaṭtu al-habl, unshiṭuhu nashṭan" means I tied it with a slip-knot, and "anshaṭtu al-habl" means I loosened it, and "anshaṭtu al-habl" also means I stretched it until it came loose. al-Farraʾ said: "unshiṭa al-ʿiqal" means it was untied, and "nushiṭa" means the rope was tied on its two hands. al-Layth said: "anshaṭtuhu bi-unshuṭah wa unshuṭatayn" means I tightened it, and "anshaṭtu al-ʿiqal" means I stretched its knot until it came loose. He said: "nashiṭa" and "anshaṭa" are two dialects with the same meaning, and on this basis Ibn ʿAbbas's earlier statement is valid. Also from him: "al-nashiṭat" are the angels, because of their vigour; they go and come by Allah's command wherever they are. Also from him, and from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both: they are the angels who draw out the spirits of the disbelievers, from between the skin and the nails, until they bring them out of their bodies with force, through distress and grief, as wool is drawn out of an iron skewer. This comes from "nashṭ," meaning pulling. It is said: "nashaṭtu al-dalw, anshiṭuhā" (with a kasra) and "anshuṭuhā" (with a damma), meaning I drew out the bucket. al-Asmaʿi said: "bi'r anshāṭ" is a well whose bottom is near, from which the bucket is drawn with one pull. "Bi'r nashūṭ" is a well from which the bucket cannot be drawn until it has been pulled many times. Mujahid said: it is death, which draws out the soul of a person. al-Suddi said: they are the souls as they are drawn out from the feet. It has also been said: "al-nazi'at" are the hands of the warriors, or their souls, which draw the bows by drawing the arrows to their utmost, and "al-nashiṭat" are those who loosen the snares. "Awhaq" (plural of "wahq," a rope with a vowel on each letter, and it may be softened) is a rope with which camels and horses are tied so that they do not bolt; a slip-knot is put at its end. ʿIkrima and ʿAta said: "al-awhaq" are the ropes that loosen the arrows. From ʿAta, Qatadah, al-Hasan and al-Akhfash also: "al-nashiṭat" are the stars, which move from one horizon to another, that is, they go. This is also in al-Sihah. "Wa al-nashiṭati nashṭan" means the stars moving from one constellation to another, like a bull that is loosed from one land to another. Anxieties also move their owner about, as Himyan ibn Qahafa said:

*My worries have come to move me about the regions,*
*Sometimes to Syria with me, sometimes to Wasit.*

Abu ʿUbayda and ʿAta also said: "al-nashiṭat" are the wild beasts when they move from one land to another, just as worries move a person from one land to another. He recited Himyan's verse: "My worries..." to the end of the line. It has also been said: "wa al-nazi'at" refers to disbelievers, and "wa al-nashiṭat" refers to believers, since the angels draw out the spirit of the believer gently, and "nazʿ" is drawing with force, while "nashṭ" is drawing gently. It has also been said: both apply to disbelievers, and the two verses after them apply to believers at the moment of leaving this world.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who glide swiftly﴾. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they are the angels who carry the spirits of the believers, gliding. al-Kalbi said: they are the angels who take the spirits of the believers, like one who swims in water: at times he dips and at times he rises. They draw them out gently and easily, then leave them so that they may rest. Mujahid and Abu Salih said: they are the angels who descend from heaven swiftly by Allah's command, as a swift horse is called "sabih" when it speeds up in its running. Also from Mujahid: the angels swim in their descent and their ascent. Also from him: "al-sabihat" is death, which swims within the souls of the children of Adam. It has also been said: they are the warhorses, as ʿAntarah said:

*And the horses know, when they swim
Into the reservoirs of death, a swim.*

Imru al-Qays said:

*Swift-running, when the racing ones grow weary,
They raise dust with their hooves over the rough ground.*

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: they are the stars that swim in their orbits, and likewise the sun and the moon. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿each in an orbit they swim﴾. ʿAta said: they are the ships that sail upon the water. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "al-sabihat" are the spirits of believers that swim with longing for the meeting with Allah and His mercy when they leave the body.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who race ahead﴾. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they are the angels who outrun the devils with revelation to the Prophets, peace be upon them. This was also said by Masruq and Mujahid. Also from Mujahid and Abu Rawq: they are the angels who outrun the son of Adam with good and righteous deeds. It has also been said: they outrun the children of Adam to righteous deeds and record them. Also from Mujahid: death outruns the human being. Muqatil said: they are the angels who carry the spirits of believers swiftly to Paradise. Ibn Masʿud said: they are the souls of believers, which race to the angels who take them, having already seen the joy, out of longing for the meeting with Allah and His mercy. Similar to this is from al-Rabiʿ, who said: they are the souls which race to leave at death. Qatadah, al-Hasan and Maʿmar said: they are the stars, some of which outrun others in their course. ʿAta said: they are the horses that race to jihad. It has also been said: "al-sabiqat" may be the spirits that outrun the bodies to Paradise or to the Fire, as al-Mawardi said. Al-Jurjani said: Allah mentioned "fa-al-sabiqat" with "fa" because it is derived from what comes before it, meaning "and those who swim, and so outrun." You say: "qama fa-dhahaba" (he stood up and so went), which means that standing up was the cause of going; but if you say "qama wa-dhahaba" (he stood up and went), standing up is not the cause of going.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 79, verses 1–14 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Then by those who arrange affairs﴾. Al-Qushayri said: They agreed that what is meant is the angels. Al-Mawardi said: There are two opinions on this. The first is that they are the angels, which is the view of the majority (al-jumhur). The second opinion is that they are the seven planets. This was related by Khalid ibn Ma'dan from Mu'adh ibn Jabal. As for their arranging affairs, there are two views. The first is that they arrange their rising and their setting. The second is that they arrange what Allah Most High has decreed concerning them of the changes of conditions. Al-Qushayri also related this view in his tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), and said that Allah Most High linked much of the arrangement of the affairs of the world to the movements of the stars, so the arrangement was attributed to them, even though it is from Allah, just as a thing is named after what is adjacent to it. And on the view that what is meant by "those who arrange" is the angels, their arranging is their bringing down of the lawful and the unlawful and its details. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others. The arranging belongs to Allah, exalted be His praise, but when the angels brought it down, they were named after it, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 193], and as He Most High said: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, for he has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97]. That is, Gabriel brought it down upon the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ), while Allah, mighty and majestic, is the One who sent it down. Ata related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿those who arrange affairs﴾: they are the angels entrusted with arranging the conditions of the earth regarding the winds, the rains and other things. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabat said: The arrangement of the affairs of this world is entrusted to four: Gabriel, Michael, the Angel of Death, whose name is 'Izra'il, and Israfil. As for Gabriel, he is entrusted with the winds and the armies. As for Michael, he is entrusted with the rain and vegetation. As for the Angel of Death, he is entrusted with seizing souls on land and sea. As for Israfil, he descends with the command to them, and no angel is closer than Israfil to the Throne, and between him and the Throne is a distance of five hundred years. It was also said: that is, they were entrusted with matters which Allah made them aware of. From the beginning of the surah up to here is an oath which Allah swore by, and Allah may swear by whatever He wills of His creation, while we have no right to do so except by Him, mighty and majestic. The answer to the oath is implied, as if He said: "By those who pull out violently, and so-and-so, you will surely be resurrected and surely be called to account." It is left implied because the listeners know its meaning, as al-Farra' said. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿When we are bones, decayed, [will we be resurrected]?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 11], which serves as the answer to their saying: ﴿When we are bones, decayed, will we be resurrected?﴾, so He suffices with His saying: ﴿When we are bones, decayed?﴾. Some people said: The oath falls upon His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 26]. This is the choice of al-Tirmidhi Ibn 'Ali, meaning: in what I have recounted of the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the mention of Moses and Pharaoh, there is indeed a lesson for whoever fears. But the oath falls upon what is mentioned clearly and openly in the surah, which is more fitting and more worthy than bringing something that is not mentioned. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is ugly, because the speech has been long between them. It was also said: the answer to the oath is ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 15], because the meaning is: it has reached you. It was also said: the answer is ﴿On the day the quaking one quakes﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 6], on the assumption of "la-yawma tarjufu" (surely on the day it quakes), and the lam was omitted. It was also said: there is inversion in it, and its estimate is: "On the day the quaking one quakes, and the following one follows, and by those who pull out violently." Al-Sijistani said: It is possible that this is from inversion, as if he said: "So they will be in the wakeful ground, and by those who pull out violently." Ibn al-Anbari said: This is an error, because the fa' is not used to begin speech, and the first is the correct view. It was also said: the oath only falls upon the hearts of the people of the Fire becoming dry and their eyes being humbled, so the accusative of ﴿on the day the quaking one quakes﴾ is according to this meaning, but it did not fall upon it. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, hearts will be trembling on the day it quakes. It was also said: it is governed by an implied "remember". ﴿Tarjufu﴾ means it is agitated. ﴿Al-Rajifah﴾ means the agitated one. This is what 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: he said it is the earth, and ﴿al-Radifah﴾ is the Hour. Mujahid said: ﴿al-Rajifah﴾ is the earthquake, and ﴿the following one follows it﴾ is the Blast. He also said, and so did Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah: they are the two Blasts, that is, the two blowings of the Trumpet. The first causes everything to die by the permission of Allah Most High, and the second brings everything to life by the permission of Allah Most High. There came in a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Between them is forty years." Mujahid also said: ﴿al-Radifah﴾ is when the sky is split and the earth and mountains are carried and crushed into one crushing, and that is after the earthquake. It was also said: ﴿al-Rajifah﴾ is the shaking of the earth, and ﴿al-Radifah﴾ is another earthquake which destroys the earths. And Allah knows best. What has passed at the end of "al-Naml" [[See vol. 13, p. 239 onwards.]] contains sufficiency regarding the blowing into the Trumpet. The root of rajfah is movement. Allah Most High said: ﴿On the day the earth quakes﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 14]. The rajfah here is not from movement alone, but from their saying: "rajafa al-ra'du yarjufu rajfan wa rajifan," meaning the thunder made its sound and its movement, and from this comes "al-arajif" (rumours), because of the agitation of voices through them and the people spreading them. He said:
"O father of rumours, O son of baseness, you threaten me, / and in the rumours I thought baseness and weakness were." [[The poem is by Manazil ibn Rabi'ah al-Munqari, in satire of Ru'bah and al-'Ajjaj. The well-known version of the line, as in the grammar books such as Sharh al-Tasrih and others, is: "O father of the rajaz poems, O son of baseness, you threaten me, / and in the rajaz poems, I thought, is baseness and weakness." "Al-arajiz" is the plural of "urjuzah," meaning poems composed in the meter of rajaz. "Wa fi al-arajiz" is the predicate preceding the subject "al-lu'm," and the interposition of "khalt" between the subject and predicate cancels its governing, which is the point of evidence in the line for the grammarians. It was also said that the accusative is not impossible, on the basis that a subject is implied, meaning "as for".]]

And from Ubayy ibn Ka'b: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to stand up when a quarter of the night had passed, and then say: "O people, remember Allah. The Quaking one has come, the following one follows it. Death has come with what is in it." [[the hadith as quoted]]

﴿Hearts on that day will be trembling﴾, that is, fearful and anxious. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and the majority of the exegetes hold this view. Al-Suddi said: moving from their places. Its parallel is: ﴿when the hearts reach the throats﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. Al-Mu'arrikh said: anxious, hasty, agitated, not still. Al-Mubarrad said: agitated. The meanings are close, and what is meant is the hearts of the disbelievers. It is said: "wajafa al-qalb yajifu wajifan," when it pounds, just as it is said: "wajaba yajibu wajiban." From this comes "wajif" of the horse and the camel when running, and "al-iyjaf" means driving a mount to a swift journey. He said:
"They were replaced after a snorting of breath with a clatter, / and after long breath with galloping."

﴿Hearts﴾ is in the nominative as the subject, and ﴿trembling﴾ is its description. ﴿Their eyes are humbled﴾ is its predicate, like His saying: ﴿a believing slave is better than an idolater﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]. The meaning of ﴿humbled﴾ is broken and abased from the terror of what they see. Its parallel is: ﴿their eyes humbled, humiliation will cover them﴾ [al-Qalam: 43]. The meaning is "the eyes of their owners", so the genitive word was omitted.

﴿They say: "Shall we indeed be returned to the former state?"﴾, that is, these deniers who reject resurrection say, when it is said to them that you will be resurrected, saying with denial and wonder: "Shall we be returned after our death to the first state, so that we return living as we were before death?" This is like their saying: ﴿Shall we indeed be raised in a new creation?﴾. It is said: "raja'a fulan fi hafiratihi" and "'ala hafiratihi," meaning he returned from where he came. This was said by Qatadah. Ibn al-A'rabi recited:
"Ahafirah 'ala salaf wa shayb / ma'adha Allah min safah wa 'ar" [meaning: "Shall I return to baldness and grey hair? God forbid from foolishness and shame!"]
He says: "Shall I return to what I was in my youth of love-poetry and youthful folly, after I have grown grey and bald?" It is also said: "raja'a 'ala hafiratihi," that is, the path by which he came. Their proverb says: "al-naqd 'inda al-hafirah" (payment is at the first word). Ya'qub said: that is, at the first word. It is also said: "al-taqa al-qawm fa-qatalu 'inda al-hafirah," that is, at the moment they first met. It was also said: al-hafirah means the worldly life, meaning: shall we indeed be returned to this world so that we live as we were? The poet said:
"I swore I would never forget you, so know this, / until people are returned to the hafirah."

It was also said: al-hafirah is the earth in which their graves are dug, so it has the meaning of "the dug-up," like His saying: ﴿created from a gushing fluid﴾ [al-Tariq: 6] and ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21]. The meaning: shall we indeed be returned to our graves alive? This was said by Mujahid, al-Khalil and al-Farra'. It was also said: the earth is called al-hafirah because it is the place where hooves rest, just as the foot is called earth because it is on the earth. The meaning: shall we indeed return after death to the earth and walk on our feet? Ibn Zayd said: al-hafirah is the Fire, and he recited: ﴿That, then, would be a losing return﴾. Muqatil and Zayd ibn Aslam said: it is one of the names of the Fire. Ibn 'Abbas said: in the language of the Arabs, al-hafirah is the world. Abu Haywah recited: "al-hafirah" without alif, a shortened form of "al-hafir." It was also said: al-hafirah is the earth filled with the bodies of its dead, from their saying: "hafirat asnanuhu," when filth settles on its outside and inside. It is said: "fi asnanihi hafar," and "qad hafirat tahfir hafran," like "kasara yaksiru kasran," when its roots are spoiled. The Bani Asad say: "fi asnanihi hafar" with vowel movement, and "qad hafira" in the pattern of "ta'iba ta'aban." This is the worse of the two dialects, said in al-Sihah.

﴿When we are bones, decayed?﴾, that is, crumbling and disintegrating. It is said: "nakhara al-'azm" (with kasra), meaning it decayed and crumbled, and it is said: "'izam nakhirah." So the majority of the people of Madinah, Makkah, Syria and Basra recited it, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred it, because when we looked at the reports that mention bones, we found "nakhirah," not "nakhirah" with alif. Abu 'Amr and his son 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn al-Zubayr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr recited "nakhirah" with alif. Al-Farra', al-Tabari and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi preferred it, as it would match the ends of verses. In al-Sihah: "al-nakhir" among bones is that into which wind enters and then comes out of it, and it has a whistling sound. It is said: "ma biha nakhir," meaning there is no one in it. Ya'qub related this from al-Bahili. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "al-nakhirah" is that which has not yet been hollowed, meaning it has not yet decayed, and it must eventually become hollow. It was also said: "al-nakhir" is the hollowed one. It was also said: they are two dialects with one meaning, just as the Arabs say: "nakhira al-shay'" so it is "nakhir" and "nakhir," like their saying: "ta'ima fa-huwa tama' wa ta'im," "hadhira fa-huwa hadhir wa hadhar," "bakhila fa-huwa bakhil wa bakhil," "rafara wa fari." The poet said:
"The old man who was once fat stays on them, / he creeps on crooked legs with the nakhirat." [[ 'Uwaj: meaning legs.]]

In some tafsir: "nakhirah" with alif means decayed, and "nakhirah" means that wind passes through it, the reverse of the first. The poet said [[the poet is al-Hamadani on the day of al-Qadisiyyah]]:
"After I became bones, hollowed (nakhirah)."
Some said: al-nakhirah is that whose extremities have been eaten and whose middles remain, and al-nakhirah is that whose entirety has spoiled. Mujahid said: nakhirah means crumbled, just as He said: ﴿bones and dust﴾ [al-Isra': 49]. The "nukhrat al-rih," with a damma, is the intensity of its blowing. Al-nukhrah also and al-nukhrah, in the pattern of al-hamzah, is the front of the nose of a horse, a donkey or a pig. It is said: "hashsham nukhratahu," meaning he crushed its nose.

﴿They said: "Then that would be a losing return"﴾, that is, a futile return, false and vain, meaning it is not a return that succeeds. This was said by al-Hasan and others. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: ﴿losing﴾ for those who denied it. It was also said: meaning it is a return of loss, and the meaning is that its people are losers, just as it is said: "a profitable trade," meaning its owner profits. There is nothing more losing than a return that leads to the Fire. Qatadah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: meaning, if we return alive after death, we will surely be gathered to the Fire, and they only said this because they had been threatened with the Fire. Al-Karr means return. It is said: "karrahu" and "karra bi-nafsihi," transitive and intransitive. Al-karrah means one time, and its plural is al-karrat.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 79, verses 1–14 (part 3 of 3):

(فَإِنَّما هِيَ زَجْرَةٌ واحِدَةٌ) ﴿Then it will be but a single shout﴾. He, exalted is His praise, mentioned the ease of the resurrection for Him, saying: ﴿Then it will be but a single shout﴾. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A single blast." ﴿And behold, they will be awake upon the Sahirah﴾, that is, upon the surface of the earth, after they had been in its belly. Al-Farra' said: "It was named this because in it is the sleep and wakefulness of living beings." The Arabs call a desert and the surface of the earth "sahirah," meaning "possessing wakefulness," because one stays awake in it out of fear of it; so He described it by a quality of what is in it. Ibn 'Abbas and the exegetes cited the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

وَفِيهَا لَحْمُ سَاهِرَةٍ وَبَحْرٍ ... وَمَا فَاهُوا بِهِ لَهُمْ مُقِيمُ

And another said on the day of Dhi Qar, to his horse:

أَقْدَمُ مَحَاجَ إِنَّهَا الْأَسَاوِرَهْ ... وَلَا يَهُولَنَّكَ رِجْلٌ [[These verses belong to al-Hamdani on the day of al-Qadisiyya, and their mention has preceded. Muhajj: the name of the poet's horse. In al-Lisan, under the root (n-kh-r): "Aqdim akhā nahm." "Wa la yahawlannaka ru'us." In al-Samin: "badirah."]] نَادِرَهْ
فَإِنَّمَا قَصْرُكَ تُرْبُ السَّاهِرَهْ ... ثُمَّ تَعُودُ بَعْدَهَا فِي الْحَافِرَهْ
مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا صِرْتَ عِظَامًا نَاخِرَهْ

In al-Sihah: It is said: "al-Sahur" is the shadow of the Sahirah, which is the surface of the earth. From this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And behold, they will be upon the Sahirah﴾. Abu Kabir al-Hudhali said:

يَرْتَدْنَ سَاهِرَةً كَأَنَّ جَمِيمَهَا ... وَعَمِيمَهَا أَسْدَافُ لَيْلٍ مُظْلِمِ [[al-Jamim, with a jim: the plant that has sprouted and risen slightly but has not fully matured; al-'Amim: the complete, fully grown plant; al-Asdaf: plural of sadf, with a fathah, which is the darkness of the night.]]

It is also said: "al-Sahur" is like a sheath for the moon, into which it enters when it is eclipsed. They recited the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt [[The first half of the verse is: "la naqsa fihi ghayra anna khabay'ah"]]:

قَمَرٌ وَسَاهُورٌ يُسَلُّ وَيُغْمَدُ

And they recited, from another, describing a woman:

كَأَنَّهَا عِرْقُ سَامٍ عِنْدَ ضَارِبِهِ ... أَوْ شُقَّةٌ [[So it is in the copies of the original that are in our hands. What is in al-Lisan, under the root (s-h-r): "aw filqah."]] خَرَجَتْ مِنْ جَوْفٍ سَاهُورٍ

He means a split of the moon. [[This is what the Arabs claimed in the pre-Islamic period.]]

It was said: al-Sahirah is the white earth. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A land of silver, upon which Allah, exalted is His praise, was never disobeyed, which He created at that time." It was said: "A land which Allah renews on the Day of Resurrection." It was said: "al-Sahirah is the name of the seventh earth, which Allah, exalted is He, will bring forth, and upon which He will call the creatures to account, and that is when the earth will be replaced by another earth." Al-Thawri said: "al-Sahirah is the land of Sham." Wahb ibn Munabbih: "A mountain of Bayt al-Maqdis." 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'Atikah: "It is the name of a specific place on earth, in Sham, the region between the mountain of Ariha' and the mountain of Hassan [[Also mentioned by al-Tabari.]], which Allah extends however He wills." Qatadah: "It is Hell," that is, "then behold, these disbelievers are in Hell." It was only called sahirah because they will not sleep upon it at that time. It was also said: "al-Sahirah" means the desert at the edge of Hell, meaning they will be made to stand in the land of the Resurrection, and wakefulness will then persist. It is also said: "al-Sahirah is the white, level land, named so because the mirage flows over it," from the saying "'ayn sahirah," meaning a spring of flowing water; its opposite is "na'imah" (sleeping). Al-Ash'ath ibn Qays said:

وَسَاهِرَةٌ يُضْحِي السَّرَابُ مُجَلِّلًا ... لِأَقْطَارِهَا قَدْ جِئْتُهَا مُتَلَثِّمَا

Or because whoever travels through it does not sleep, out of fear of perishing.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 79, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 3):**

Surah al-Nazi'at is Meccan by scholarly consensus (ijma'). It has forty-five or forty-six verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By those who drag out with violence, and those who draw out gently, and those who glide swiftly, and those who race ahead, and those who direct affairs. On the day when the quaking one quakes, followed by the following one. Hearts that day will be trembling, their eyes humbled.﴾

﴿They say: "Shall we indeed be returned to our former state? Even when we are decayed bones?" They say: "That would then be a losing return." But it will be only one shout, and at once they will be on the surface of the earth.﴾

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿By those who drag out with violence﴾. He swears by these things He mentioned that the Resurrection is true. "Those who drag out" (al-nazi'at) are the angels who pull out the souls of the disbelievers. This was said by ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him. Likewise Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Masruq and Mujahid said: they are the angels who pull out the souls of the children of Adam. Ibn Masʿud said: he means the souls of the disbelievers, which the Angel of Death pulls out of their bodies from beneath every hair and beneath the nails and the soles of the feet, pulling them out like a skewer pulled from wet wool. "Ighraq" means he drowns them, that is, he sends them back into their bodies, then pulls them out again; this is his work with the disbelievers. Ibn ʿAbbas said the same. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: their spirits are pulled out, then drowned, then burned, then cast into the Fire. It has also been said: the disbeliever sees his soul at the time of its extraction as if it were drowning. al-Suddi said: "those who drag out" are the souls as they sink into the chests. Mujahid said: it is death, which pulls out the souls. al-Hasan and Qatadah said: they are the stars, which are drawn from one horizon to another, meaning they move, from the expression "nazaʿa ilayhi" (he went toward it), or from the expression "nazaʿat al-khayl" (the horses ran). "Gharqan" means they sink, set, and rise from one horizon to another. This was said by Abu ʿUbayda, Ibn Kaysan and al-Akhfash. It has also been said: "those who drag out" are bows, which draw the arrows. This was said by ʿAta and ʿIkrima. "Gharqan" means "ighraqan" (drawing to the utmost). Drawing a bow to its utmost (ighraq) means pulling it until it reaches its full extent, until it reaches the arrowhead. It is said: "aghraqa fi al-qawsi," meaning he completed its draw, which happens when the string reaches the notch next to the arrowhead, around which it is wound. "Al-istighraq" means full comprehensiveness. The inner membrane of an eggshell is called "ghirqi'." It has also been said: they are the warriors who shoot arrows. I say: this and the previous interpretation amount to the same thing, because when He swears by the bows, what is meant is those who draw them, in honour of them. This is like His saying: ﴿By the charging steeds, panting﴾ [al-ʿAdiyat: 1]. And Allah knows best. By "ighraq" He intended exaggeration in drawing, and this applies to all the interpretations of it. It has also been said: they are wild animals that drag away from the pasture and flee. This was related by Yahya ibn Salam. The meaning of "gharqan" is then: going far away while drawing.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who draw out gently﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: this means the angels who ease the soul of the believer and take it, as a tether is loosed from the foot of a camel when it is untied. al-Farraʾ related this view and then said: what I have heard from the Arabs is that they say "unshitat" (it was loosed), and "ka-annama unshita min ʿiqal" (as if it were loosed from a tether). Its binding is its "nashṭ" (tying), and the one who ties is "nashit"; when you tie a rope to a camel's foot, you have "nashatah," so you are "nashit," and when you untie it, you have "anshatah," and you are "munshit." Also from Ibn ʿAbbas: they are the souls of believers at death, which become eager to leave, because no believer is facing death without Paradise being shown to him before he dies, so he sees what Allah has prepared for him of wives and family, the dark-eyed houris. They call him to it, so his soul is eager to leave and go to them. Also from him, he said: this means the souls of disbelievers and hypocrites, which are drawn out as the sinew is drawn out from which the arrow is strung. "Al-ʿaqab," with a vowel on the first letter, is the sinew from which bowstrings are made, singular "ʿaqabah." It is said of it: "ʿaqaba al-sahm wa al-qadah wa al-qaws ʿaqban," meaning he wound something of it around it. "Al-nashṭ" is pulling quickly. From it comes "al-unshuṭah," a knot that is easily loosened when pulled, like the knot of a belt. Abu Zayd said: "nashaṭtu al-habl, unshiṭuhu nashṭan" means I tied it with a slip-knot, and "anshaṭtu al-habl" means I loosened it, and "anshaṭtu al-habl" also means I stretched it until it came loose. al-Farraʾ said: "unshiṭa al-ʿiqal" means it was untied, and "nushiṭa" means the rope was tied on its two hands. al-Layth said: "anshaṭtuhu bi-unshuṭah wa unshuṭatayn" means I tightened it, and "anshaṭtu al-ʿiqal" means I stretched its knot until it came loose. He said: "nashiṭa" and "anshaṭa" are two dialects with the same meaning, and on this basis Ibn ʿAbbas's earlier statement is valid. Also from him: "al-nashiṭat" are the angels, because of their vigour; they go and come by Allah's command wherever they are. Also from him, and from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both: they are the angels who draw out the spirits of the disbelievers, from between the skin and the nails, until they bring them out of their bodies with force, through distress and grief, as wool is drawn out of an iron skewer. This comes from "nashṭ," meaning pulling. It is said: "nashaṭtu al-dalw, anshiṭuhā" (with a kasra) and "anshuṭuhā" (with a damma), meaning I drew out the bucket. al-Asmaʿi said: "bi'r anshāṭ" is a well whose bottom is near, from which the bucket is drawn with one pull. "Bi'r nashūṭ" is a well from which the bucket cannot be drawn until it has been pulled many times. Mujahid said: it is death, which draws out the soul of a person. al-Suddi said: they are the souls as they are drawn out from the feet. It has also been said: "al-nazi'at" are the hands of the warriors, or their souls, which draw the bows by drawing the arrows to their utmost, and "al-nashiṭat" are those who loosen the snares. "Awhaq" (plural of "wahq," a rope with a vowel on each letter, and it may be softened) is a rope with which camels and horses are tied so that they do not bolt; a slip-knot is put at its end. ʿIkrima and ʿAta said: "al-awhaq" are the ropes that loosen the arrows. From ʿAta, Qatadah, al-Hasan and al-Akhfash also: "al-nashiṭat" are the stars, which move from one horizon to another, that is, they go. This is also in al-Sihah. "Wa al-nashiṭati nashṭan" means the stars moving from one constellation to another, like a bull that is loosed from one land to another. Anxieties also move their owner about, as Himyan ibn Qahafa said:

*My worries have come to move me about the regions,*
*Sometimes to Syria with me, sometimes to Wasit.*

Abu ʿUbayda and ʿAta also said: "al-nashiṭat" are the wild beasts when they move from one land to another, just as worries move a person from one land to another. He recited Himyan's verse: "My worries..." to the end of the line. It has also been said: "wa al-nazi'at" refers to disbelievers, and "wa al-nashiṭat" refers to believers, since the angels draw out the spirit of the believer gently, and "nazʿ" is drawing with force, while "nashṭ" is drawing gently. It has also been said: both apply to disbelievers, and the two verses after them apply to believers at the moment of leaving this world.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who glide swiftly﴾. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they are the angels who carry the spirits of the believers, gliding. al-Kalbi said: they are the angels who take the spirits of the believers, like one who swims in water: at times he dips and at times he rises. They draw them out gently and easily, then leave them so that they may rest. Mujahid and Abu Salih said: they are the angels who descend from heaven swiftly by Allah's command, as a swift horse is called "sabih" when it speeds up in its running. Also from Mujahid: the angels swim in their descent and their ascent. Also from him: "al-sabihat" is death, which swims within the souls of the children of Adam. It has also been said: they are the warhorses, as ʿAntarah said:

*And the horses know, when they swim
Into the reservoirs of death, a swim.*

Imru al-Qays said:

*Swift-running, when the racing ones grow weary,
They raise dust with their hooves over the rough ground.*

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: they are the stars that swim in their orbits, and likewise the sun and the moon. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿each in an orbit they swim﴾. ʿAta said: they are the ships that sail upon the water. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "al-sabihat" are the spirits of believers that swim with longing for the meeting with Allah and His mercy when they leave the body.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who race ahead﴾. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they are the angels who outrun the devils with revelation to the Prophets, peace be upon them. This was also said by Masruq and Mujahid. Also from Mujahid and Abu Rawq: they are the angels who outrun the son of Adam with good and righteous deeds. It has also been said: they outrun the children of Adam to righteous deeds and record them. Also from Mujahid: death outruns the human being. Muqatil said: they are the angels who carry the spirits of believers swiftly to Paradise. Ibn Masʿud said: they are the souls of believers, which race to the angels who take them, having already seen the joy, out of longing for the meeting with Allah and His mercy. Similar to this is from al-Rabiʿ, who said: they are the souls which race to leave at death. Qatadah, al-Hasan and Maʿmar said: they are the stars, some of which outrun others in their course. ʿAta said: they are the horses that race to jihad. It has also been said: "al-sabiqat" may be the spirits that outrun the bodies to Paradise or to the Fire, as al-Mawardi said. Al-Jurjani said: Allah mentioned "fa-al-sabiqat" with "fa" because it is derived from what comes before it, meaning "and those who swim, and so outrun." You say: "qama fa-dhahaba" (he stood up and so went), which means that standing up was the cause of going; but if you say "qama wa-dhahaba" (he stood up and went), standing up is not the cause of going.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 79, verses 1–14 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Then by those who arrange affairs﴾. Al-Qushayri said: They agreed that what is meant is the angels. Al-Mawardi said: There are two opinions on this. The first is that they are the angels, which is the view of the majority (al-jumhur). The second opinion is that they are the seven planets. This was related by Khalid ibn Ma'dan from Mu'adh ibn Jabal. As for their arranging affairs, there are two views. The first is that they arrange their rising and their setting. The second is that they arrange what Allah Most High has decreed concerning them of the changes of conditions. Al-Qushayri also related this view in his tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), and said that Allah Most High linked much of the arrangement of the affairs of the world to the movements of the stars, so the arrangement was attributed to them, even though it is from Allah, just as a thing is named after what is adjacent to it. And on the view that what is meant by "those who arrange" is the angels, their arranging is their bringing down of the lawful and the unlawful and its details. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others. The arranging belongs to Allah, exalted be His praise, but when the angels brought it down, they were named after it, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 193], and as He Most High said: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, for he has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97]. That is, Gabriel brought it down upon the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ), while Allah, mighty and majestic, is the One who sent it down. Ata related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿those who arrange affairs﴾: they are the angels entrusted with arranging the conditions of the earth regarding the winds, the rains and other things. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabat said: The arrangement of the affairs of this world is entrusted to four: Gabriel, Michael, the Angel of Death, whose name is 'Izra'il, and Israfil. As for Gabriel, he is entrusted with the winds and the armies. As for Michael, he is entrusted with the rain and vegetation. As for the Angel of Death, he is entrusted with seizing souls on land and sea. As for Israfil, he descends with the command to them, and no angel is closer than Israfil to the Throne, and between him and the Throne is a distance of five hundred years. It was also said: that is, they were entrusted with matters which Allah made them aware of. From the beginning of the surah up to here is an oath which Allah swore by, and Allah may swear by whatever He wills of His creation, while we have no right to do so except by Him, mighty and majestic. The answer to the oath is implied, as if He said: "By those who pull out violently, and so-and-so, you will surely be resurrected and surely be called to account." It is left implied because the listeners know its meaning, as al-Farra' said. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿When we are bones, decayed, [will we be resurrected]?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 11], which serves as the answer to their saying: ﴿When we are bones, decayed, will we be resurrected?﴾, so He suffices with His saying: ﴿When we are bones, decayed?﴾. Some people said: The oath falls upon His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 26]. This is the choice of al-Tirmidhi Ibn 'Ali, meaning: in what I have recounted of the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the mention of Moses and Pharaoh, there is indeed a lesson for whoever fears. But the oath falls upon what is mentioned clearly and openly in the surah, which is more fitting and more worthy than bringing something that is not mentioned. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is ugly, because the speech has been long between them. It was also said: the answer to the oath is ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 15], because the meaning is: it has reached you. It was also said: the answer is ﴿On the day the quaking one quakes﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 6], on the assumption of "la-yawma tarjufu" (surely on the day it quakes), and the lam was omitted. It was also said: there is inversion in it, and its estimate is: "On the day the quaking one quakes, and the following one follows, and by those who pull out violently." Al-Sijistani said: It is possible that this is from inversion, as if he said: "So they will be in the wakeful ground, and by those who pull out violently." Ibn al-Anbari said: This is an error, because the fa' is not used to begin speech, and the first is the correct view. It was also said: the oath only falls upon the hearts of the people of the Fire becoming dry and their eyes being humbled, so the accusative of ﴿on the day the quaking one quakes﴾ is according to this meaning, but it did not fall upon it. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, hearts will be trembling on the day it quakes. It was also said: it is governed by an implied "remember". ﴿Tarjufu﴾ means it is agitated. ﴿Al-Rajifah﴾ means the agitated one. This is what 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: he said it is the earth, and ﴿al-Radifah﴾ is the Hour. Mujahid said: ﴿al-Rajifah﴾ is the earthquake, and ﴿the following one follows it﴾ is the Blast. He also said, and so did Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah: they are the two Blasts, that is, the two blowings of the Trumpet. The first causes everything to die by the permission of Allah Most High, and the second brings everything to life by the permission of Allah Most High. There came in a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Between them is forty years." Mujahid also said: ﴿al-Radifah﴾ is when the sky is split and the earth and mountains are carried and crushed into one crushing, and that is after the earthquake. It was also said: ﴿al-Rajifah﴾ is the shaking of the earth, and ﴿al-Radifah﴾ is another earthquake which destroys the earths. And Allah knows best. What has passed at the end of "al-Naml" [[See vol. 13, p. 239 onwards.]] contains sufficiency regarding the blowing into the Trumpet. The root of rajfah is movement. Allah Most High said: ﴿On the day the earth quakes﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 14]. The rajfah here is not from movement alone, but from their saying: "rajafa al-ra'du yarjufu rajfan wa rajifan," meaning the thunder made its sound and its movement, and from this comes "al-arajif" (rumours), because of the agitation of voices through them and the people spreading them. He said:
"O father of rumours, O son of baseness, you threaten me, / and in the rumours I thought baseness and weakness were." [[The poem is by Manazil ibn Rabi'ah al-Munqari, in satire of Ru'bah and al-'Ajjaj. The well-known version of the line, as in the grammar books such as Sharh al-Tasrih and others, is: "O father of the rajaz poems, O son of baseness, you threaten me, / and in the rajaz poems, I thought, is baseness and weakness." "Al-arajiz" is the plural of "urjuzah," meaning poems composed in the meter of rajaz. "Wa fi al-arajiz" is the predicate preceding the subject "al-lu'm," and the interposition of "khalt" between the subject and predicate cancels its governing, which is the point of evidence in the line for the grammarians. It was also said that the accusative is not impossible, on the basis that a subject is implied, meaning "as for".]]

And from Ubayy ibn Ka'b: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to stand up when a quarter of the night had passed, and then say: "O people, remember Allah. The Quaking one has come, the following one follows it. Death has come with what is in it." [[the hadith as quoted]]

﴿Hearts on that day will be trembling﴾, that is, fearful and anxious. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and the majority of the exegetes hold this view. Al-Suddi said: moving from their places. Its parallel is: ﴿when the hearts reach the throats﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. Al-Mu'arrikh said: anxious, hasty, agitated, not still. Al-Mubarrad said: agitated. The meanings are close, and what is meant is the hearts of the disbelievers. It is said: "wajafa al-qalb yajifu wajifan," when it pounds, just as it is said: "wajaba yajibu wajiban." From this comes "wajif" of the horse and the camel when running, and "al-iyjaf" means driving a mount to a swift journey. He said:
"They were replaced after a snorting of breath with a clatter, / and after long breath with galloping."

﴿Hearts﴾ is in the nominative as the subject, and ﴿trembling﴾ is its description. ﴿Their eyes are humbled﴾ is its predicate, like His saying: ﴿a believing slave is better than an idolater﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]. The meaning of ﴿humbled﴾ is broken and abased from the terror of what they see. Its parallel is: ﴿their eyes humbled, humiliation will cover them﴾ [al-Qalam: 43]. The meaning is "the eyes of their owners", so the genitive word was omitted.

﴿They say: "Shall we indeed be returned to the former state?"﴾, that is, these deniers who reject resurrection say, when it is said to them that you will be resurrected, saying with denial and wonder: "Shall we be returned after our death to the first state, so that we return living as we were before death?" This is like their saying: ﴿Shall we indeed be raised in a new creation?﴾. It is said: "raja'a fulan fi hafiratihi" and "'ala hafiratihi," meaning he returned from where he came. This was said by Qatadah. Ibn al-A'rabi recited:
"Ahafirah 'ala salaf wa shayb / ma'adha Allah min safah wa 'ar" [meaning: "Shall I return to baldness and grey hair? God forbid from foolishness and shame!"]
He says: "Shall I return to what I was in my youth of love-poetry and youthful folly, after I have grown grey and bald?" It is also said: "raja'a 'ala hafiratihi," that is, the path by which he came. Their proverb says: "al-naqd 'inda al-hafirah" (payment is at the first word). Ya'qub said: that is, at the first word. It is also said: "al-taqa al-qawm fa-qatalu 'inda al-hafirah," that is, at the moment they first met. It was also said: al-hafirah means the worldly life, meaning: shall we indeed be returned to this world so that we live as we were? The poet said:
"I swore I would never forget you, so know this, / until people are returned to the hafirah."

It was also said: al-hafirah is the earth in which their graves are dug, so it has the meaning of "the dug-up," like His saying: ﴿created from a gushing fluid﴾ [al-Tariq: 6] and ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21].
