"Al-arajiz" is the plural of "urjuzah," meaning poems composed in the meter of rajaz. "Wa fi al-arajiz" is the predicate preceding the subject "al-lu'm," and the interposition of "khalt" between the subject and predicate cancels its governing, which is the point of evidence in the line for the grammarians. It was also said that the accusative is not impossible, on the basis that a subject is implied, meaning "as for".]]

And from Ubayy ibn Ka'b: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to stand up when a quarter of the night had passed, and then say: "O people, remember Allah. The Quaking one has come, the following one follows it. Death has come with what is in it." [[the hadith as quoted]]

﴿Hearts on that day will be trembling﴾, that is, fearful and anxious. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and the majority of the exegetes hold this view. Al-Suddi said: moving from their places. Its parallel is: ﴿when the hearts reach the throats﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. Al-Mu'arrikh said: anxious, hasty, agitated, not still. Al-Mubarrad said: agitated. The meanings are close, and what is meant is the hearts of the disbelievers. It is said: "wajafa al-qalb yajifu wajifan," when it pounds, just as it is said: "wajaba yajibu wajiban." From this comes "wajif" of the horse and the camel when running, and "al-iyjaf" means driving a mount to a swift journey. He said:
"They were replaced after a snorting of breath with a clatter, / and after long breath with galloping."

﴿Hearts﴾ is in the nominative as the subject, and ﴿trembling﴾ is its description. ﴿Their eyes are humbled﴾ is its predicate, like His saying: ﴿a believing slave is better than an idolater﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]. The meaning of ﴿humbled﴾ is broken and abased from the terror of what they see. Its parallel is: ﴿their eyes humbled, humiliation will cover them﴾ [al-Qalam: 43]. The meaning is "the eyes of their owners", so the genitive word was omitted.

﴿They say: "Shall we indeed be returned to the former state?"﴾, that is, these deniers who reject resurrection say, when it is said to them that you will be resurrected, saying with denial and wonder: "Shall we be returned after our death to the first state, so that we return living as we were before death?" This is like their saying: ﴿Shall we indeed be raised in a new creation?﴾. It is said: "raja'a fulan fi hafiratihi" and "'ala hafiratihi," meaning he returned from where he came. This was said by Qatadah. Ibn al-A'rabi recited:
"Ahafirah 'ala salaf wa shayb / ma'adha Allah min safah wa 'ar" [meaning: "Shall I return to baldness and grey hair? God forbid from foolishness and shame!"]
He says: "Shall I return to what I was in my youth of love-poetry and youthful folly, after I have grown grey and bald?" It is also said: "raja'a 'ala hafiratihi," that is, the path by which he came. Their proverb says: "al-naqd 'inda al-hafirah" (payment is at the first word). Ya'qub said: that is, at the first word. It is also said: "al-taqa al-qawm fa-qatalu 'inda al-hafirah," that is, at the moment they first met. It was also said: al-hafirah means the worldly life, meaning: shall we indeed be returned to this world so that we live as we were? The poet said:
"I swore I would never forget you, so know this, / until people are returned to the hafirah."

It was also said: al-hafirah is the earth in which their graves are dug, so it has the meaning of "the dug-up," like His saying: ﴿created from a gushing fluid﴾ [al-Tariq: 6] and ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21]. The meaning: shall we indeed be returned to our graves alive? This was said by Mujahid, al-Khalil and al-Farra'. It was also said: the earth is called al-hafirah because it is the place where hooves rest, just as the foot is called earth because it is on the earth. The meaning: shall we indeed return after death to the earth and walk on our feet? Ibn Zayd said: al-hafirah is the Fire, and he recited: ﴿That, then, would be a losing return﴾. Muqatil and Zayd ibn Aslam said: it is one of the names of the Fire. Ibn 'Abbas said: in the language of the Arabs, al-hafirah is the world. Abu Haywah recited: "al-hafirah" without alif, a shortened form of "al-hafir." It was also said: al-hafirah is the earth filled with the bodies of its dead, from their saying: "hafirat asnanuhu," when filth settles on its outside and inside. It is said: "fi asnanihi hafar," and "qad hafirat tahfir hafran," like "kasara yaksiru kasran," when its roots are spoiled. The Bani Asad say: "fi asnanihi hafar" with vowel movement, and "qad hafira" in the pattern of "ta'iba ta'aban." This is the worse of the two dialects, said in al-Sihah.

﴿When we are bones, decayed?﴾, that is, crumbling and disintegrating. It is said: "nakhara al-'azm" (with kasra), meaning it decayed and crumbled, and it is said: "'izam nakhirah." So the majority of the people of Madinah, Makkah, Syria and Basra recited it, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred it, because when we looked at the reports that mention bones, we found "nakhirah," not "nakhirah" with alif. Abu 'Amr and his son 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn al-Zubayr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr recited "nakhirah" with alif. Al-Farra', al-Tabari and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi preferred it, as it would match the ends of verses. In al-Sihah: "al-nakhir" among bones is that into which wind enters and then comes out of it, and it has a whistling sound. It is said: "ma biha nakhir," meaning there is no one in it. Ya'qub related this from al-Bahili. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "al-nakhirah" is that which has not yet been hollowed, meaning it has not yet decayed, and it must eventually become hollow. It was also said: "al-nakhir" is the hollowed one. It was also said: they are two dialects with one meaning, just as the Arabs say: "nakhira al-shay'" so it is "nakhir" and "nakhir," like their saying: "ta'ima fa-huwa tama' wa ta'im," "hadhira fa-huwa hadhir wa hadhar," "bakhila fa-huwa bakhil wa bakhil," "rafara wa fari." The poet said:
"The old man who was once fat stays on them, / he creeps on crooked legs with the nakhirat." [[ 'Uwaj: meaning legs.]]

In some tafsir: "nakhirah" with alif means decayed, and "nakhirah" means that wind passes through it, the reverse of the first. The poet said [[the poet is al-Hamadani on the day of al-Qadisiyyah]]:
"After I became bones, hollowed (nakhirah)."
Some said: al-nakhirah is that whose extremities have been eaten and whose middles remain, and al-nakhirah is that whose entirety has spoiled. Mujahid said: nakhirah means crumbled, just as He said: ﴿bones and dust﴾ [al-Isra': 49]. The "nukhrat al-rih," with a damma, is the intensity of its blowing. Al-nukhrah also and al-nukhrah, in the pattern of al-hamzah, is the front of the nose of a horse, a donkey or a pig. It is said: "hashsham nukhratahu," meaning he crushed its nose.

﴿They said: "Then that would be a losing return"﴾, that is, a futile return, false and vain, meaning it is not a return that succeeds. This was said by al-Hasan and others. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: ﴿losing﴾ for those who denied it. It was also said: meaning it is a return of loss, and the meaning is that its people are losers, just as it is said: "a profitable trade," meaning its owner profits. There is nothing more losing than a return that leads to the Fire. Qatadah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: meaning, if we return alive after death, we will surely be gathered to the Fire, and they only said this because they had been threatened with the Fire. Al-Karr means return. It is said: "karrahu" and "karra bi-nafsihi," transitive and intransitive. Al-karrah means one time, and its plural is al-karrat.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 79, verses 1–14 (part 3 of 3):

(فَإِنَّما هِيَ زَجْرَةٌ واحِدَةٌ) ﴿Then it will be but a single shout﴾. He, exalted is His praise, mentioned the ease of the resurrection for Him, saying: ﴿Then it will be but a single shout﴾. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A single blast." ﴿And behold, they will be awake upon the Sahirah﴾, that is, upon the surface of the earth, after they had been in its belly. Al-Farra' said: "It was named this because in it is the sleep and wakefulness of living beings." The Arabs call a desert and the surface of the earth "sahirah," meaning "possessing wakefulness," because one stays awake in it out of fear of it; so He described it by a quality of what is in it. Ibn 'Abbas and the exegetes cited the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

وَفِيهَا لَحْمُ سَاهِرَةٍ وَبَحْرٍ ... وَمَا فَاهُوا بِهِ لَهُمْ مُقِيمُ

And another said on the day of Dhi Qar, to his horse:

أَقْدَمُ مَحَاجَ إِنَّهَا الْأَسَاوِرَهْ ... وَلَا يَهُولَنَّكَ رِجْلٌ [[These verses belong to al-Hamdani on the day of al-Qadisiyya, and their mention has preceded. Muhajj: the name of the poet's horse. In al-Lisan, under the root (n-kh-r): "Aqdim akhā nahm." "Wa la yahawlannaka ru'us." In al-Samin: "badirah."]] نَادِرَهْ
فَإِنَّمَا قَصْرُكَ تُرْبُ السَّاهِرَهْ ... ثُمَّ تَعُودُ بَعْدَهَا فِي الْحَافِرَهْ
مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا صِرْتَ عِظَامًا نَاخِرَهْ

In al-Sihah: It is said: "al-Sahur" is the shadow of the Sahirah, which is the surface of the earth. From this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And behold, they will be upon the Sahirah﴾. Abu Kabir al-Hudhali said:

يَرْتَدْنَ سَاهِرَةً كَأَنَّ جَمِيمَهَا ... وَعَمِيمَهَا أَسْدَافُ لَيْلٍ مُظْلِمِ [[al-Jamim, with a jim: the plant that has sprouted and risen slightly but has not fully matured; al-'Amim: the complete, fully grown plant; al-Asdaf: plural of sadf, with a fathah, which is the darkness of the night.]]

It is also said: "al-Sahur" is like a sheath for the moon, into which it enters when it is eclipsed. They recited the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt [[The first half of the verse is: "la naqsa fihi ghayra anna khabay'ah"]]:

قَمَرٌ وَسَاهُورٌ يُسَلُّ وَيُغْمَدُ

And they recited, from another, describing a woman:

كَأَنَّهَا عِرْقُ سَامٍ عِنْدَ ضَارِبِهِ ... أَوْ شُقَّةٌ [[So it is in the copies of the original that are in our hands. What is in al-Lisan, under the root (s-h-r): "aw filqah."]] خَرَجَتْ مِنْ جَوْفٍ سَاهُورٍ

He means a split of the moon. [[This is what the Arabs claimed in the pre-Islamic period.]]

It was said: al-Sahirah is the white earth. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A land of silver, upon which Allah, exalted is His praise, was never disobeyed, which He created at that time." It was said: "A land which Allah renews on the Day of Resurrection." It was said: "al-Sahirah is the name of the seventh earth, which Allah, exalted is He, will bring forth, and upon which He will call the creatures to account, and that is when the earth will be replaced by another earth." Al-Thawri said: "al-Sahirah is the land of Sham." Wahb ibn Munabbih: "A mountain of Bayt al-Maqdis." 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'Atikah: "It is the name of a specific place on earth, in Sham, the region between the mountain of Ariha' and the mountain of Hassan [[Also mentioned by al-Tabari.]], which Allah extends however He wills." Qatadah: "It is Hell," that is, "then behold, these disbelievers are in Hell." It was only called sahirah because they will not sleep upon it at that time. It was also said: "al-Sahirah" means the desert at the edge of Hell, meaning they will be made to stand in the land of the Resurrection, and wakefulness will then persist. It is also said: "al-Sahirah is the white, level land, named so because the mirage flows over it," from the saying "'ayn sahirah," meaning a spring of flowing water; its opposite is "na'imah" (sleeping). Al-Ash'ath ibn Qays said:

وَسَاهِرَةٌ يُضْحِي السَّرَابُ مُجَلِّلًا ... لِأَقْطَارِهَا قَدْ جِئْتُهَا مُتَلَثِّمَا

Or because whoever travels through it does not sleep, out of fear of perishing.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 79, verses 15–26:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Has the story of Musa reached you? When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa﴾. That is, the story of Musa has come to you and reached you. This is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: Pharaoh was stronger than the disbelievers of your time, then We seized him, and so will these. It was also said: "hal" here means "ma," that is, "what has come to you," but you have been informed of it, for in it is a lesson for whoever fears (Allah). The story of Musa and Pharaoh has already passed in more than one place with what is sufficient [[See vol. 7, p. 256 ff., vol. 11, p. 200 ff., and vol. 13, p. 250 ff.]].

As for "Tuwa," there are three readings. Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans read "Tuwan" with tanwin, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this for the lightness of the name. The rest read it without tanwin, because it is a diptote (ma'dul), like 'Umar and Quthám. Al-Farra' said: Tuwa is a valley between Madinah and Egypt. He said: It is a diptote derived from "tawin," just as 'Umar is derived from "'Amir." Al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah read "Tiwan" with a kasra on the ta', and it is reported from Abu 'Amr, meaning "sacred" repeated again and again, as al-Zajjaj said, and he recited:

"O blamer, indeed the blame is not in its proper place upon me, a repeated folly of your wandering error."
[[The speaker is 'Adi ibn Zayd.]]

That is, it is repeated blame upon me. It was also said that the dammah and the kasrah on the ta' are two dialects, and the discussion of it has passed in Surat Ta-Ha.

﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾, that is, his Lord called to him, and the verb is omitted because calling is a speech, so it is as if He said to him: "Your Lord says: Go to Pharaoh." ﴿He has indeed transgressed﴾, that is, he exceeded all measure in disobedience. It is related from al-Hasan who said: Pharaoh was a man of Hamadan. From Mujahid who said: He was from the people of Istakhr. And from al-Hasan also, who said: He was from the people of Isfahan, and he was called Dhu Zufr, whose length was four spans.

﴿So say: Would you like to purify yourself﴾, that is, would you submit and be cleansed of sins? Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "Would you like to bear witness that there is no god but Allah?"

﴿And I would guide you to your Lord﴾, that is, I would direct you to obedience to your Lord, ﴿so you would fear (Him)﴾, that is, you would dread Him and be mindful of Him. Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "tazakka" with a shaddah on the zay, by assimilating the ta' into the zay, since its original form is "tatazakka." The rest read "tazakka" with the zay unshaddah, meaning the ta' is dropped. Abu 'Amr said: "tazakka" with shaddah [[The addition is from al-Tabari and is necessary.]] [...] "tatasaddaq" [...] and "tazakka" means to become pure and a believer. He only invited Pharaoh so that he would become pure and a believer. He said: For this reason we have chosen the lighter reading. Sakhr ibn Juwayriyah said: When Allah sent Musa to Pharaoh, He said to him: "Go to Pharaoh" up to His saying "and I would guide you to your Lord so you would fear (Him)," but he will not do it. Musa said: "O Lord, how can I go to him when You know that he will not do it?" Allah revealed to him: "Proceed to what I have commanded you, for in the heaven there are twelve thousand angels who seek the knowledge of the decree, and they have not reached it nor attained it."

﴿Then he showed him the greatest sign﴾, that is, the greatest proof, which is the miracle. It was said: it is the staff. It was said: it is the white hand shining like the sun. Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas: "The greatest sign" is the staff. Al-Hasan said: his hand and his staff. It was also said: the splitting of the sea. And it was said: "the sign" refers to all of His signs and miracles. ﴿But he denied and disobeyed﴾, that is, he denied the Prophet of Allah Musa and disobeyed his Lord, mighty and majestic.

﴿Then he turned his back, striving﴾, that is, he withdrew, turning away from faith, ﴿striving﴾, that is, working at corruption on the earth. It was also said: he worked to harm Musa. It was said: he turned his back, running away from the serpent. ﴿Then he gathered (his people)﴾, that is, he assembled his companions to protect him from it. It was said: he gathered his soldiers for fighting and war, and the magicians for opposition. It was said: he gathered the people to attend. ﴿Then he called out﴾, that is, he said to them in a loud voice: ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾, that is, there is no lord above me for you. It is narrated that Iblis appeared to Pharaoh in human form in Egypt, in the bathhouse, and Pharaoh did not recognize him. Iblis said to him: "Woe to you! Do you not know me?" He said: "No." He said: "How, when you created me? Did you not say, 'I am your Lord, the Most High'?" Al-Tha'labi mentioned this in his book "al-'Ara'is." 'Ata' said: He had made small idols for them and ordered them to worship them, so he said, "I am the lord of your idols." It was also said: he meant the leaders and the masters; he is their lord, and those are the lords of the base people. It was also said: there is an inversion in the speech, so that "he called out" comes before "he gathered," because the calling comes before the gathering.

﴿So Allah seized him, (as) an example for the Hereafter and the former (life)﴾, that is, as a punishment for his saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than myself﴾ [al-Qasas: 38], and his later saying: ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24]. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said this. Between the two statements there were forty years, as Ibn 'Abbas said. The meaning is: He gave him respite for the first, then seized him for the last, and punished him for both of his statements. It was also said: the punishment of the first is that He drowned him, and the punishment of the last is the punishment in the Hereafter. Qatadah and others said this. Mujahid said: it is the punishment of the beginning and end of his life. It was also said: the last statement is "I am your Lord, the Most High," and the first is his denial of Musa, also from Qatadah.

"Nakal" is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun according to al-Zajjaj, because the meaning of "akhadhahu Allah" is "Allah made an example of him," so a verbal noun derived from its meaning, not from its wording, was brought in its place. It was also said: it is in the accusative by removing the preposition of description, meaning "Allah seized him with the example of the Hereafter," and when the preposition was removed it became accusative. Al-Farra' said: that is, Allah seized him with a seizing that is a punishment, meaning for the punishment. "Nakal" is a name for what is made into a deterrent for others, that is, a punishment for him so that one may take warning from it. It is said: "nakkala fulan bi-fulan" when he inflicted severe punishment upon him. The root carries the sense of restraint, and from it comes "nukul" (refusal) to take an oath, and "nikl" (shackle). It has already passed in Surat al-Muzzammil [[See p. 45 of this part.]], and praise belongs to Allah.

﴿Indeed in that is a lesson﴾, that is, a consideration and an admonition, ﴿for whoever fears﴾, that is, fears Allah, mighty and majestic.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 79, verses 27–33:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is the heaven?﴾ He means the people of Makkah: Is your creation after death more difficult in your estimation, or the heaven? Whoever has power over the heaven has power over the restoration. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir: 57], and His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81]. So the meaning of the statement is reproach and rebuke. Then He described the heaven, saying: ﴿He raised its vault﴾, i.e., He raised it above you like a building. ﴿He raised its vault﴾, i.e., He elevated its ceiling in the air. It is said: "I raised (samaktu) the thing," i.e., I lifted it into the air, and "the thing rose high (samaka) with a sumuk," i.e., it was elevated. Al-Farra' said: everything that carries something of a building or other than it is a samk (roof-beam/support). A "masmuk building" and a "samik tamik hump" mean high. The "al-musmakat" (in the lexicon it is "al-musmakat," like "mukarramat," and it is so reported in a hadith; al-Taj affirmed that "al-musmakat" is correct Arabic, not a solecism, and the hadith is also reported by another route) means: the heavens. It is also said: "ismuk fi al-Daym," i.e., ascend to the rank.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He made it level﴾, i.e., He created it in a level form, with no disparity in it, no cracks, and no fissures.

﴿And He darkened its night﴾, i.e., He made it dark. Ghatisha al-layl and Aghtasha-hu Allah: like your saying, "Dhalima al-layl" [the night was dark] and "Adhlamahu Allah" [God darkened it]. It is also said: "Aghtasha al-layl bi-nafsihi" [the night darkened by itself], and "Aghtasha-hu Allah" just as one says "Adhlama al-layl" and "Adhlamahu Allah." Al-ghatash and al-ghabash mean darkness. A man who is aghtash is blind or like one who is blind, and he has become ghatish; a woman is ghatsha'; it is said: "a night that is ghatsha'," "a ghatsh night" and "a ghatsha desert" in which one cannot find the way. Al-A'sha said:

*"And a bewildering desert in the night, its wilderness dark, the call of its owl is company to me."*

*(Al-fayyad, with the fa' vowelled either way: the male owl.)*

Al-A'sha also said:

*"I slaughtered for them my she-camel at the watering place, and their night-covering is pitch-dark and ghatish."*

He means by "their night-covering" their night, because it covers them with its blackness. He attributed the night to the heaven, because the night occurs with the setting of the sun, and the sun is attached to the heaven. And it is said: "the stars of the night," because they appear at night.

﴿And He brought forth its forenoon﴾, i.e., He made its daylight, its brightness, and its sun appear. He attributed the forenoon (ad-duha) to the heaven just as He attributed the night to it, because in it is the cause of darkness and light, which is the setting and rising of the sun.

﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾, i.e., He spread it out. This points to the earth being after the heaven. The discussion of this has already passed at the beginning of al-Baqarah [vol. 1, p. 255] at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth; then He turned to the heaven﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29], in full.

The Arabs say: "Dahawtu al-shay' adhuhu dahwan," meaning: I spread the thing out. It is said that the ostrich's nest is "udhaiyy," because it is spread out on the surface of the earth. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

*"And He scattered creation upon it when He spread it out, so they are its inhabitants until the calling-out (of the Day)."*

(This line passed in vol. 15, p. 310 with the wording "sukkanuha" [its inhabitants]; the meaning is the same.)

Al-Mubarrad recited:

*"He spread it out, and when He saw it level, upon the water He set the mountains firm over it."*

It is also said: "daha-ha" means "sawwa-ha" (He made it even). From this is the saying of Zayd ibn Amr:

*"I submitted my face to Him to whom the earth submits, bearing heavy stones."*

*"He spread it out, and when it became level He made it firm with hands, and set the mountains upon it."*

It is reported from Ibn Abbas: God created the Ka'bah and placed it on the water upon four pillars, a thousand years before He created the world; then the earth was spread out from beneath the House. Some scholars mention that "ba'da" here is in the place of "ma'a" (with), as if He said: "and the earth with that He spread out," just as He said, exalted is He: ﴿Violent, and after that, ill-born﴾ [al-Qalam: 13]. ﴿The day man will remember what he strove for﴾, that is, what he did of good or evil. ﴿And Hell is made manifest to whoever sees﴾, that is, it becomes visible. It was also said: the believer sees it so that he may know the value of the blessing, and the disbeliever is burned by the Fire. Malik ibn Dinar recited: "wa-burrizat al-jahim." 'Ikrimah and others read: "li-man tara" with the ta', meaning for whom Hell is seen, or for whom you, O Muhammad, see it. The address is to him, peace be upon him, and the intended meaning is the people.

The Exalted said: ﴿So when the Greatest Calamity comes﴾, that is, the great catastrophe, which is the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thaniyah), by which resurrection will occur. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of al-Dahhak from him, and it is the view of al-Hasan. And from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak as well: it is the Resurrection (al-qiyamah). It was so named because it overwhelms everything (tatummu 'ala kulli shay'), so it covers whatever is other than it, due to the magnitude of its terror, that is, it overturns it. And among their proverbs:

"The valley flowed and overflowed the qara" [[al-qara: the channel of water in a meadow; the plural is aqra'ah, aqra' and qiryan. The proverb is used when something exceeds its limit.]]

Al-Mubarrad said: al-tammah, among the Arabs, is the calamity that cannot be withstood. It was derived, as I think, from their saying: tamma al-faras tamiman when the horse exhausts its effort in running, and tamma al-ma' when the water fills the entire river. Others said: it is derived from tamma al-sayl al-rakiyyah [[al-rakiyyah: the well; i.e., the flood of the valley covered it.]], that is, it buried it, and al-tamm means burying and rising above. Al-Qasim ibn al-Walid al-Hamdani said: the Greatest Calamity is when the people of Paradise are driven to Paradise and the people of the Fire to the Fire. This is the meaning of the statement of Mujahid. Sufyan said: it is the hour in which the people of the Fire are handed over to the Zabaniyah. That is, it is the calamity that overwhelms and becomes great. He said:

"Indeed some love blinds and deafens,
and likewise hatred is more calamitous and overwhelming."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 79, verse 37–41:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿As for him who transgressed and preferred the worldly life﴾, meaning he exceeded the limit in disobedience. It has been said: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr and his son al-Harith, but it is general for every disbeliever who preferred the worldly life over the Hereafter. It is narrated from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir that he said: whoever makes three kinds of dishes from one food has transgressed. Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak that he said: Hudhayfah said: "What I fear most for this Ummah is that they will prefer what they see over what they know" [in T: "what they act upon"]. It is also reported that it was found in the books: God, mighty and majestic is He, said: "None of My servants prefers his worldly life over his Hereafter except that I scatter his worries upon him and ruin him [in some copies: and rob him of his gains], and then I do not care in which of them he perishes."

(﴿Then indeed Hellfire is the refuge﴾), meaning his refuge. The definite article here replaces the pronoun.

(﴿But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord﴾), meaning he feared standing before his Lord. Al-Rabi' said: his standing on the Day of Reckoning. Qatadah used to say: "Indeed, God has a standing which the believers feared." Mujahid said: it is his fear, in this world, of God, mighty and majestic, when he is about to commit a sin, so he desists. Its parallel is: ﴿And for him who feared the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46].

(﴿And restrained the soul from desire﴾), meaning he restrained it from sins and prohibited things. Sahl said: abandoning desire is the key to Paradise, based on the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire﴾. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "You are in a time when the truth leads desire; but a time will come when desire will lead the truth, so we seek refuge in God from that time."

(﴿Then indeed Paradise is the refuge﴾), meaning the abode. The two verses were revealed concerning Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr and his brother 'Amir ibn 'Umayr. al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "As for 'He who transgressed,' it refers to a brother of Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr who was captured on the day of Badr. The Ansar seized him and said: 'Who are you?' He said: 'I am the brother of Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr.' They did not bind him tightly, honored him, and lodged him with them. When morning came, they told Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr about his situation. He said: 'He is not a brother to me. Bind your captive tightly, for his mother is the richest person in al-Batha' in ornaments and wealth.' So they bound him until his mother sent for his ransom. As for 'He who feared the standing before his Lord,' it refers to Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, who shielded the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with himself on the day of Uhud when the people scattered away from him, until the arrows (mashaqis, meaning arrows) pierced his body. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw him writhing in his blood, he said: [I reckon you before God]. He said to his companions: [I saw him wearing two cloaks whose value could not be known, and the straps of his sandals were of gold]." It has also been said that Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr killed his brother 'Amir on the day of Badr. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: this verse was revealed concerning two men: Abu Jahl ibn Hisham al-Makhzumi and Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr al-'Abdari. al-Suddi said: this verse, "But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord," was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may God be pleased with him). Abu Bakr had a servant who brought him food, and he used to ask him where he obtained it. One day the servant brought him food and he did not ask, and he ate it. The servant said to him: "Why did you not ask me today?" He said: "I forgot." Then he said: "Where did this food come from?" He replied: "I practiced fortune-telling for some people in the Jahiliyyah, and they gave me this." Abu Bakr immediately vomited it up and said: "O Lord, nothing remains in the veins, for You have held it back." Then this was revealed: ﴿But as for him who feared the standing before his Lord﴾. Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning one who intended a sin and was able to commit it in private, then abandoned it out of fear of God. Something similar is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. That is, one who, at the moment of sin, feared his standing before God and so refrained. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 79, verses 42–46:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They ask you about the Hour, when will it take place?﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: The polytheists of Makkah asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the Hour would come, mockingly, so Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed the verse. 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said, regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿What have you to do with mentioning it?﴾: The Prophet (ﷺ) kept being asked about the Hour until this verse was revealed: ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾. The meaning of mursaha (its settling) is its establishment (qiyamuha). Al-Farra' said: its rusuw (settling) is its qiyam (establishment), like your saying "qama al-'adl" and "qama al-haqq" (justice and truth stood), meaning they became manifest and firm, like the anchoring of a ship (rusuw al-safinah). Abu 'Ubaydah said: it means its finality (muntaha), and the anchorage of a ship (marsa al-safinah) is the place where it comes to rest; this is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: when its time is. The meanings are close. Its explanation has already passed in "al-A'raf" (see vol. 8, p. 335 onward). It is narrated from al-Hasan that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Hour will not come except with an outburst of anger that your Lord will display."
